tagline: Understand the threat. Master the defense.
description: A free, practical cybersecurity awareness academy: learn how attacks work, how they are detected, and how defenders respond — then practice in a safe game arena.

domains.blurb: How attackers manipulate people rather than machines.
Ransomware, trojans, worms, and fileless techniques.
Injection, broken access control, and the OWASP Top 10.
Rogue access points, Bluetooth, and device botnets.
Misconfigurations, leaked keys, and over-broad identity.
Credential reuse, spraying, MFA abuse, and session theft.
Trusted access misused, plus physical and people risks.
Compromising vendors and dependencies to reach many victims.
APTs, zero-days, lateral movement, and exfiltration.
Device loss, malicious apps, and mobile lures.
Deepfakes, synthetic phishing, and prompt injection.
Encryption, hashing, keys, and protecting data at rest.

tips: Treat urgency as a warning sign: scammers want you to act before you think.
Use a password manager so every account can have a unique password.
An unexpected MFA prompt is an attack until proven otherwise — deny and report.
Verify payment or bank-detail changes using a phone number you already trust.
Update your router and IoT devices; default passwords are an open door.
On public Wi-Fi, confirm the network name with staff and keep HTTPS on.
A familiar voice or face can be generated. Verify the request, not the medium.

selfCheck.q: I use a different password for every important account.
selfCheck.tip: A password manager makes unique passwords effortless.

selfCheck.q: I have multi-factor authentication enabled on my email.
selfCheck.tip: Email is the reset key for everything else — protect it with MFA.

selfCheck.q: I check the sender and link destination before clicking.
selfCheck.tip: Hover to preview links; type known addresses yourself when in doubt.

selfCheck.q: My devices and apps are set to update automatically.
selfCheck.tip: Patch management closes the doors attackers love most.

selfCheck.q: I know how to report a suspicious message at work or school.
selfCheck.tip: Fast reporting protects everyone — make sure the path is obvious.

socRoles.name: L1 Analyst
socRoles.text: First responder to alerts. Validates signals, enriches context, escalates true positives, and documents decisions.

socRoles.name: L2 Analyst
socRoles.text: Deep-dives into incidents, correlates logs across sources, hunts for scope, and recommends containment.

socRoles.name: L3 Analyst
socRoles.text: Owns complex investigations, reverse-engineers suspicious artifacts, and tunes detection engineering.

socRoles.name: Threat Hunter
socRoles.text: Builds hypotheses from intelligence and searches telemetry for activity that automation missed.

socRoles.name: IR Lead
socRoles.text: Runs the incident bridge, makes containment decisions, manages communications, and drives lessons learned.

lifecycle.name: Preparation
lifecycle.text: Build the team, playbooks, tooling, telemetry, and relationships before an incident. Define severity levels and communication paths.
lifecycle.outputs: IR plan, contacts, runbooks, access to logs

lifecycle.name: Detection & Analysis
lifecycle.text: Alerts arrive from SIEM, EDR, email, and users. Analysts validate, scope, and classify the event.

lifecycle.name: Containment
lifecycle.text: Stop further damage: isolate hosts, revoke sessions, block domains. Short-term containment buys time for durable fixes.

lifecycle.name: Eradication
lifecycle.text: Remove the root cause — malicious files, accounts, persistence, and vulnerable configurations.

lifecycle.name: Recovery
lifecycle.text: Restore services from known-good backups, validate operations, and monitor closely for regression.

lifecycle.name: Lessons Learned
lifecycle.text: Blameless review: what happened, what worked, what to change. Feed updates back into preparation.

layers.name: Identity
layers.text: MFA, least privilege, strong passwords, conditional access.

layers.name: Endpoint
layers.text: EDR, patching, hardening baselines, application control.

layers.name: Application
layers.text: Secure coding, SAST/DAST, WAF, API gateway.

principles.name: Defense in depth
principles.text: Layer controls so one failure does not mean total compromise.

principles.name: Zero Trust
principles.text: Never trust by network location alone; verify every request, device, and identity.

principles.name: Least privilege
principles.text: Grant only the access needed, only for as long as it is needed.

principles.name: Patch management
principles.text: Inventory, prioritize by exposure, test, deploy, and verify.

principles.name: Backups
principles.text: Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two media, one offline/immutable, and test restores.

teams.name: Red Team
teams.text: Simulates adversaries to test detection and response, under strict authorization.

teams.name: Blue Team
teams.text: Defends daily: monitors, investigates, hardens, and responds.

teams.name: Purple Team
teams.text: Bridges both: runs exercises and turns findings into measurable detection improvements.

frameworks.name: NIST CSF
frameworks.text: Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. A flexible outcome-based framework.

frameworks.name: ISO/IEC 27001
frameworks.text: Requirements for an information security management system (ISMS), with risk-based controls.

frameworks.name: CIS Controls
frameworks.text: Prioritized, practical safeguards such as asset inventory and MFA — great starting point.

frameworks.name: GDPR
frameworks.text: EU privacy regulation: lawful processing, data minimization, rights, and breach notification duties.

frameworks.name: MITRE ATT&CK
frameworks.text: A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used to map detections and gaps.

glossary.def: Evidence that suggests an intrusion occurred, such as a malicious hash, domain, IP, or unusual account behavior.
A platform that collects and correlates logs from many systems to support detection, investigation, and compliance.
Tooling that records endpoint behavior and can isolate a machine during an incident.

glossary.full: Adversary Tactics and Techniques knowledge base
glossary.def: A public framework describing how attackers operate, used to map detections and gaps.
Requiring two or more proofs of identity, such as a password plus a device-bound key.
A model where no user or device is trusted by default, even inside the network; every request is verified.
An email policy that tells receivers how to handle messages failing SPF/DKIM checks.
Giving accounts and systems only the permissions required for their legitimate task.
A model of attack stages from reconnaissance through actions on objectives.
A phishing-resistant login credential bound to a specific site and stored on a device or security key.
A hidden way for an attacker to return to a system without repeating the original compromise.
Unauthorized transfer of data out of an organization.
A group of compromised devices controlled remotely, often used for DDoS or spam.
Faking a sender, address, or identity so traffic appears to come from a trusted source.
Reducing attack surface by disabling unnecessary features, changing defaults, and applying secure settings.

timeline.title: XSS worm goes viral
timeline.text: A self-propagating script showed that browser-side flaws can spread at internet speed.

timeline.title: RSA SecurID breach
timeline.text: A targeted phishing email with an attachment led to a landmark supply-chain-style compromise.

timeline.title: Mirai botnet & Dyn DDoS
timeline.text: Default-credential IoT devices disrupted major internet services.

timeline.title: WannaCry ransomware
timeline.text: A wormable strain exploited unpatched systems worldwide.

timeline.title: SolarWinds supply chain
timeline.text: A signed software update became the delivery vehicle for a long-running intrusion.

timeline.title: Colonial Pipeline
timeline.text: A compromised remote-access credential preceded a disruptive ransomware incident.

timeline.title: AI voice clone fraud
timeline.text: Synthetic voices were used to impersonate executives in payment fraud schemes.

timeline.title: Identity is the new perimeter
timeline.text: Passkeys, phishing-resistant MFA, and behavior detection define modern defense.

threatMap.text: Tailored email lures are the most reported synthetic signal in this region.
Payment-change requests dominate the sample, usually through compromised mailboxes.
Double-extortion reports lead the simulated activity in this region.
Reused passwords and automated login attempts drive the sample signal.
Short availability attacks are the most common simulated network event.
Vendor and dependency compromise accounts for the highest-impact sample cases.
Delivery-fee texts and fake payment links lead the mobile-lure sample.
Misclassified storage and over-broad roles appear most often in the sample.
